analysis.one_liner: Bans pyramid schemes that pay people mainly for recruiting others, enforced by the FTC.
analysis.headline: The Anti-Pyramid Promotional Scheme Act was introduced with 30 cosponsors in May 2016, referred to committee, and never received any vote before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful, with the Federal Trade Commission enforcing it, to run a "pyramid promotional scheme" — a plan that pays people primarily for signing up new participants rather than for selling products to actual customers. It spells out exactly what counts as a pyramid scheme, requires companies to buy back unsold inventory at no less than 90% of cost within 12 months, and treats violations as deceptive practices under existing FTC law. It was never voted on in committee or on the floor.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, consumers recruited into schemes where earnings come mainly from recruitment would gain a federal statute to fall back on, and the FTC would get a written definition to enforce. Honest direct-selling companies competing against outright recruitment scams would also benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to establish, operate, or promote a pyramid promotional scheme — a plan where compensation comes primarily from recruiting new participants rather than selling products to ultimate users.
Gives the FTC explicit enforcement power, treating violations as unfair or deceptive acts under the Federal Trade Commission Act.

Requires companies to repurchase current, marketable unsold inventory at not less than 90% of the participant's original net cost within 12 months, limiting the practice of loading recruits up with unsellable stock.

analysis.who_pays: Multi-level marketing companies whose business depends on recruiting distributors who buy product would bear new compliance costs, a mandatory 90% inventory buyback obligation, and FTC enforcement exposure — though the bill's own definitions would still count product bought by participants for personal use as legitimate sales.

drawbacks.text: The definition counts a participant as an "ultimate user" when they buy "reasonable amounts" of product for personal use, so under the mechanics of multi-level marketing — where much revenue comes from the salesforce itself buying inventory and products to stay qualified — a scheme could meet the letter of this law while still earning substantially from its own recruits' purchases rather than outside customers.

The buyback guarantee only covers inventory not clearly described in advance as discounted, seasonal, or promotional, giving companies a written route to avoid repurchasing exactly the stock most likely to be unsellable.

Writing a precise pyramid definition into statute would freeze what is now flexible case-by-case enforcement into a fixed legal standard; companies that fit the statutory definition would gain a safe harbor, a change whose practical significance depends heavily on how narrowly the definitions are drawn.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated ban would help people caught in recruitment-driven schemes, but the FTC already polices pyramid schemes under its existing deception authority, so the bill's main practical change would have been to lock a specific definition into law. On the text itself, that definition — counting participants' own purchases as sales and limiting buybacks — would have protected the mainstream multi-level marketing model at least as much as it punished outright scams. A stronger bill would have closed both gaps.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2016 and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee, and it sat there until the Congress ended with no vote at any stage.

narrative.text: Rep. Marsha Blackburn introduced the bill on May 13, 2016, joined by Rep. Marc Veasey, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the same day.
On May 20, 2016, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or a Senate companion vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the FTC's existing, broader case-by-case authority over pyramid schemes was left untouched, and the direct-selling industry did not get the statutory definitions critics warned would shield mainstream multi-level marketing companies. Consumers lost nothing that FTC enforcement had not already been providing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: FTC kept its broader enforcement power

for.name: Marsha Blackburn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Anti-Pyramid Promotional Scheme Act of 2016 in the House.

for.name: Marc Veasey
for.what_they_did: Joined Blackburn as the bill's original cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: Direct Selling Association
for.role: Trade group for multi-level marketing companies
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed the bill as a federal standard for the direct-selling industry.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never advanced it; it sat at the subcommittee level with no markup or vote for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Edith Ramirez
against.what_they_did: Publicly warned that the bill's definitions would hamper the FTC's ability to stop pyramid schemes, after the agency had just obtained a major settlement against a large multi-level marketing company.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — 30 cosponsors split 21 Republicans and 9 Democrats — and no vote was ever taken on the bill, so the record shows no partisan opposition bloc.

industries.note: The bill would ban outright recruitment-driven pyramids while writing the mainstream multi-level marketing model into law: compensation from product bought by participants for personal use counts as sales to "ultimate users," and inventory buybacks are capped by the bill's own definitions. That would entrench the industry's recruiting-based revenue structure even as the bill regulates it, and critics warned it would shield major companies from the FTC's broader case-by-case enforcement.
Schemes that pay participants mainly for recruiting others would be explicitly unlawful, with FTC enforcement on top of existing law. Their loss would be ordinary people's gain.
